title: A Game of Polo with a Headless Goat
author: Emma Levine
blurb: A chaotic and funny account of a donkey race in Karachi. Vivid description captures the thrilling anarchy of the event.
source: Levine writes about a donkey race in Karachi, Pakistan
heading: From A Game of Polo with a Headless Goat - Emma Levine
context: Levine travelled throughout Asia researching and filming unusual sports. In this passage she writes about a donkey race in Karachi, Pakistan.

paragraphs.html: We drove off to find the best viewing spot, which turned out to be the crest of the hill so we could see the approaching race. I asked the lads if we could join in the 'Wacky Races' and follow the donkeys, and they loved the idea. 'We'll open the car boot, you climb inside and point your camera towards the race. As the donkeys overtake us, we'll join the cars.' 'But will you try and get to the front?' 'Oh yes, that's no problem.'

The two lads who had never been interested in this Karachi sport were suddenly fired up with enthusiasm. We waited for eternity on the brow of the hill, me perched in the boot with a zoom lens pointing out. Nearly one hour later I was beginning to feel rather silly when the only action was a villager on a wobbly bicycle, who nearly fell off as he cycled past and gazed around at us.

Several vehicles went past, and some donkey-carts carrying spectators. 'Are they coming?' we called out to them. 'Coming, coming,' came the reply. I was beginning to lose faith in its happening, but the lads remained confident.

Just as I was assuming that the race had been cancelled, we spotted two approaching donkey-carts in front of a cloud of fumes and dust created by some fifty vehicles roaring up in their wake. As they drew nearer, Yaqoob revved up the engine and began to inch the car out of the lay-by. The two donkeys were almost dwarfed by their entourage; but there was no denying their speed — the Kibla donkey is said to achieve speeds of up to 40 kph, and this looked close. The two were neck-and-neck, their jockeys perched on top of the tiny carts using their whips energetically, although not cruelly.

The noise of the approaching vehicles grew; horns tooting, bells ringing, and the special rattles used just for this purpose (like maracas, a metal container filled with dried beans). Men standing on top of their cars and vans, hanging out of taxis and perched on lorries, all cheered and shouted, while the vehicles jostled to get to the front of the convoy.

Yaqoob chose exactly the right moment to edge out of the road and swerve in front of the nearest car, finding the perfect place to see the two donkeys and at the front of the vehicles. This was Formula One without rules, or a city-centre rush hour gone anarchic; a complete flouting of every type of traffic rule and common sense.

Our young driver relished this unusual test of driving skills. It was survival of the fittest, and depended upon the ability to cut in front of a vehicle with a sharp flick of the steering wheel (no lane discipline here); quick reflexes to spot a gap in the traffic for a couple of seconds; nerves of steel, and an effective horn. There were two races — the motorized spectators at the back; in front, the two donkeys, still running close and amazingly not put off by the uproar just behind them. Ahead of the donkeys, oncoming traffic — for it was a main road — had to dive into the ditch and wait there until we had passed. Yaqoob loved it. We stayed near to the front, his hand permanently on the horn and his language growing more colourful with every vehicle that tried to cut in front. ...

The road straightened and levelled, and everyone picked up speed as we neared the end of the race. But just as they were reaching the finishing line, the hospital gate, there was a near pile-up as the leading donkey swerved, lost his footing and he and the cart tumbled over. The race was over.

And then the trouble began. I assumed the winner was the one who completed the race but it was not seen that way by everyone. Apart from the two jockeys and 'officials' (who, it turned out, were actually monitoring the race) there were over a hundred punters who had all staked money on the race, and therefore had strong opinions. Some were claiming that the donkey had fallen because the other one had been ridden too close to him. Voices were raised, fists were out and tempers rising. Everyone gathered around one jockey and official, while the bookmakers were trying to insist that the race should be re-run.

Yaqoob and Iqbal were nervous of hanging around a volatile situation. They agreed to find out for me what was happening, ordering me to stay inside the car as they were swallowed up by the crowd. They emerged some time later. 'It's still not resolved,' said Iqbal, 'but it's starting to get nasty. I think we should leave.' As we drove away, Yaqoob reflected on his driving skills. 'I really enjoyed that,' he said as we drove off at a more sedate pace. 'But I don't even have my licence yet because I'm underage!'

They both found this hilarious, but I was glad he hadn't told me before; an inexperienced, underage driver causing a massive pile-up in the middle of the high-stakes donkey race could have caused problems.

wacky-races.what: This allusion (a familiar reference) points to a 1960s cartoon of silly, rule-free car races.
wacky-races.effect: Readers instantly picture comic chaos, so a strange event abroad feels familiar and funny.

try-front.quote: But will you try and get to the front?
try-front.what: Levine asks for the front, the most exciting and dangerous place to film from.
try-front.effect: We see her as bold and a little reckless, and her keenness pulls us in.

no-problem.what: The lads' cheerful 'no problem' makes racing through busy traffic sound easy.
no-problem.effect: This foreshadows trouble: their breezy confidence will be tested, and the driver turns out to be underage.

never-interested.what: Levine sets a low starting point: the lads had never cared about donkey racing.
never-interested.effect: Their sudden excitement then feels bigger and funnier.

suddenly-fired.what: 'Fired up' compares their excitement to an engine starting, and 'suddenly' shows how fast they change.
suddenly-fired.effect: We see that a race's thrill is catching, even for people who were bored.

eternity.what: 'Eternity' means forever, yet the real wait was about an hour.
eternity.effect: The joke shows her impatience and stretches the build-up, so the race feels more explosive when it comes.

perched-boot.quote: perched in the boot with a zoom lens pointing out
perched-boot.what: 'Perched' makes Levine sound like a bird balanced in the car boot.
perched-boot.effect: She is happy to look silly to get her shot, which makes her likeable.

rather-silly.what: 'Rather silly' is a mild, very British phrase for feeling foolish.
rather-silly.effect: Her gentle self-mockery makes us like and trust her.

wobbly-bicycle.what: The only 'action' is one wobbly cyclist: bathos (a drop from grand to silly).
wobbly-bicycle.effect: We laugh at the let-down, and the quiet makes the later noise more shocking.

coming-coming.what: The doubled word reassures but gives no real information about when.
coming-coming.effect: We share Levine's frustration as the locals stay relaxed and she waits for a clear answer.

lose-faith.what: 'Lose faith' is a weighty phrase, as if she were doubting a belief.
lose-faith.effect: It raises tension, and the grand phrase is comically serious for a donkey race.

remained-confident.what: Levine sets her own doubt against the lads' calm, and 'remained' shows they never wavered.
remained-confident.effect: She honestly admits that the insiders understand this event better than she does.

cloud-fumes.what: The race first appears as fumes and dust, which we almost smell and taste.
cloud-fumes.effect: The convoy arrives like a storm, hiding the donkeys: the cars will take over.

roaring-wake.what: A 'wake' is the wave behind a ship, here made by fifty vehicles behind two carts.
roaring-wake.effect: We picture a huge, noisy wave of traffic surging behind two tiny donkeys.

revved-up.what: 'Revved up' brings the engine's sound into the scene, like a racing driver on the starting line.
revved-up.effect: We feel the tension of the moment just before the chase begins.

inch-car.what: To 'inch' is to move very slowly, Yaqoob's last calm movement before the wild driving.
inch-car.effect: The slow verb holds the action back, so the speed that follows feels faster.

almost-dwarfed.what: 'Dwarfed' means made to look tiny, and an 'entourage' is the crowd that follows a celebrity.
almost-dwarfed.effect: The donkeys become comic stars, almost swamped by their own fans.

40-kph.what: Levine gives a precise speed, then checks it herself: 'this looked close'.
40-kph.effect: The fact surprises us, since we think of donkeys as slow, and makes her account feel trustworthy.

neck-and-neck.what: 'Neck-and-neck' is a horse-racing phrase for a very close contest.
neck-and-neck.effect: It treats the donkey race as a serious sport and builds excitement, as we cannot tell who will win.

energetically-not-cruelly.what: Levine expects readers to worry about the whips and answers that worry at once.
energetically-not-cruelly.effect: She stays fair to the jockeys, and we can enjoy the race without feeling guilty.

horns-bells.what: Levine lists sounds in matching pairs, and 'tooting' is onomatopoeia (a word that sounds like its meaning).
horns-bells.effect: The quick phrases pile up, so we almost hear the din growing.

like-maracas.quote: like maracas, a metal container filled with dried beans
like-maracas.what: Levine compares the local rattles to 'maracas' to explain an unfamiliar object.
like-maracas.effect: It shows she is writing for British or Western readers, who can now picture and hear it.

standing-hanging.quote: standing on top of their cars and vans, hanging out of taxis and perched on lorries
standing-hanging.what: Each verb, 'standing', 'hanging', 'perched', puts a man in a risky spot on a moving vehicle.
standing-hanging.effect: The list sweeps across the crowd, and nobody seems to care about safety.

jostled.what: 'Jostled' usually describes people pushing in a crowd, but here the vehicles shove.
jostled.effect: The cars seem to share the rough eagerness of their drivers.

exactly-right.what: 'Exactly' and 'perfect' show Levine is impressed by Yaqoob's timing.
exactly-right.effect: Once we learn he has no licence, this praise becomes both funny and alarming.

formula-one.what: Formula One is built on strict rules, so Levine keeps the speed and removes the rules.
formula-one.effect: The phrase sounds almost like a contradiction, which matches the madness of the scene.

rush-hour-anarchic.what: 'Anarchic' means lawless, applied to the ordinary city traffic most readers know.
rush-hour-anarchic.effect: Imagining familiar rush hour with every rule removed helps us feel the danger.

complete-flouting.quote: complete flouting of every type of traffic rule and common sense
complete-flouting.what: To 'flout' is to break openly, and 'complete' and 'every type' allow no exceptions.
complete-flouting.effect: It sounds like a telling-off, yet Levine is clearly enjoying herself.

relished.what: To 'relish' is to enjoy with great pleasure, like a tasty meal.
relished.effect: Yaqoob's glee hints at youthful recklessness, which pays off when we learn his age.

survival-fittest.what: This phrase from the theory of evolution turns a main road into a wild animal struggle.
survival-fittest.effect: Using a grand scientific phrase for a donkey race is part of the joke.

sharp-flick.what: 'Flick' suggests a tiny, fast movement of the wrist.
sharp-flick.effect: The light word makes a risky swerve sound casual, yet shows real skill.

no-lane.what: The bracketed aside sounds like a calm remark from a driving instructor.
no-lane.effect: The phrase is far too mild for the chaos, and that gap is the joke.

nerves-steel.what: 'Nerves of steel' sits in a list of driving skills that ends with 'an effective horn'.
nerves-steel.effect: The drop from real courage to a car horn is a comic letdown.

two-races.what: Levine splits the scene: donkeys race in front and the spectators' cars race behind.
two-races.effect: The joke is that the watchers' race has become wilder than the real one.

amazingly-not.what: 'Amazingly' shows Levine's surprise that the donkeys ignore the uproar behind them.
amazingly-not.effect: The donkeys seem more sensible than the humans, a quiet joke at the crowd's expense.

dive-ditch.what: 'Dive' makes oncoming cars sound like people leaping for safety.
dive-ditch.effect: We see the real danger to ordinary drivers, though Levine reports it lightly.

yaqoob-loved.what: Three plain words stand alone after long sentences packed with action.
yaqoob-loved.effect: The short sentence lands like a punchline, putting Yaqoob's simple joy centre stage.

permanently-horn.what: 'Permanently' exaggerates how often Yaqoob uses the horn, though perhaps not by much.
permanently-horn.effect: We hear an endless blast of noise and sense his pushy driving style.

more-colourful.what: This euphemism (a gentle word for something rude) means Yaqoob swears more and more.
more-colourful.effect: We fill in the bad language ourselves, which is funnier.

near-pile-up.what: A 'pile-up' is a crash of many vehicles, the moment of highest drama.
near-pile-up.effect: 'Near' keeps us on edge, since disaster is only just avoided.

swerved-tumbled.quote: swerved, lost his footing and he and the cart tumbled over
swerved-tumbled.what: Each verb, 'swerved', 'lost his footing', 'tumbled', is one step in the fall.
swerved-tumbled.effect: We watch the crash in slow motion, and soft 'tumbled' keeps the tone light.

race-over.what: Four blunt words follow a long sentence describing the crash.
race-over.effect: The abrupt stop mirrors the race ending, and sets up the surprise in the next line.

trouble-began.what: 'And then' opens a new paragraph like a storyteller: the race is over, the story is not.
trouble-began.effect: 'Trouble' is vague, so we read on to find out what it is.

hundred-punters.quote: over a hundred punters who had all staked money
hundred-punters.what: 'Punters' are people who bet, and over a hundred have money on this race.
hundred-punters.effect: This explains why tempers rise so fast.

strong-opinions.what: 'Strong opinions' is a mild way to describe a furious crowd.
strong-opinions.effect: The calm phrase is comic, since fists are soon out.

voices-raised.quote: Voices were raised, fists were out and tempers rising
voices-raised.what: Three quick clauses (a tricolon) each name a new sign of trouble.
voices-raised.effect: The fast rhythm mirrors how quickly things get out of hand, and 'fists' signals violence.

nervous-hanging.what: The fearless lads from the race are now 'nervous'.
nervous-hanging.effect: If even locals want to leave, we know the danger is real.

volatile-situation.what: 'Volatile' describes chemicals that can explode easily.
volatile-situation.effect: We feel the angry crowd could blow up at any moment.

swallowed-crowd.what: 'Swallowed up' turns the crowd into a huge creature that eats the lads.
swallowed-crowd.effect: We share Levine's worry as she waits alone in the car.

getting-nasty.quote: but it's starting to get nasty. I think we should leave
getting-nasty.what: Iqbal's short, plain sentences make 'nasty' a clear warning from someone who knows the area.
getting-nasty.effect: The calm, direct advice creates urgency.

really-enjoyed.what: Yaqoob's happy comment comes as they drive at a calm, 'sedate' pace.
really-enjoyed.effect: The calm lets us breathe before the shock in his next line.

dont-licence.quote: But I don't even have my licence yet because I'm underage!
dont-licence.what: Levine saves the biggest surprise for last: their skilful driver is underage.
dont-licence.effect: We look back at the wild chase with new horror, and his 'driving skills' become a joke.

hilarious.what: 'Hilarious' shows the lads laughing hard, while Levine is quietly worried.
hilarious.effect: The gap is funny, and may reflect their youth or a different attitude to risk.

glad-hadnt.quote: glad he hadn't told me before
glad-hadnt.what: Levine must have been shocked, yet says only that she was 'glad'.
glad-hadnt.effect: We laugh at her restraint and share her relief.

massive-pile-up.what: This echoes the 'near pile-up' at the finish, imagining a worse version.
massive-pile-up.effect: Ending with 'could have caused problems', a huge understatement, leaves us laughing at the danger.

high-stakes.what: 'High-stakes' usually describes big-money gambles, yet here it sits next to 'donkey race'.
high-stakes.effect: The clash is funny but true: real money and real tempers rode on this race.

entourage.meaning: A group of people who follow and look after someone important.
entourage.note: Celebrities and royalty have an entourage. Levine uses it as a joke for the vehicles following two donkeys.
entourage.effect: The donkeys become comic celebrities. The grand word makes the scene funnier.

overview.heading: Why Levine wrote this
overview.intro: Levine writes to inform her readers and to entertain them.

points.label: To share unusual sports
points.text: "researching and filming unusual sports" shows she travels to find and record events most readers will never see.

points.label: To entertain with chaos
points.text: "Formula One without rules" turns a local donkey race into a thrilling, funny spectacle.

points.label: To show a different culture
points.text: "high-stakes donkey race" shows how much the event matters locally, with real money riding on it.

overview.heading: Who she is writing for
overview.intro: Levine writes for British and Western readers who enjoy travel and humour.

points.label: Readers at home
points.text: "Wacky Races" and "Formula One" are familiar references that help readers picture an unfamiliar event.

points.label: Travel lovers
points.text: Details of Karachi's roads, crowds and noise let readers experience a place they may never visit.

points.label: Readers who want to laugh
points.text: "like maracas" explains a strange object in a light, friendly way.

overview.heading: How her tone changes
overview.intro: Her tone shifts as the day moves from waiting to danger.

points.label: Eager to join in
points.text: "But will you try and get to the front?" shows she wants to be in the thick of the action.

points.label: Laughing at herself
points.text: "rather silly" shows her poking fun at herself as the wait drags on.

points.label: Thrilled passenger
points.text: "Yaqoob loved it" shows her sharing the driver's excitement.

points.label: Relieved survivor
points.text: "glad he hadn't told me before" shows her looking back, shaken, at the danger she was in.

overview.heading: Language choices
overview.intro: Levine's word choices help readers see and hear the chaos.

points.label: Racing comparisons
points.text: "Formula One without rules" and "neck-and-neck" use racing language to make the chaos easy to picture.

points.label: Noise
points.text: "horns tooting, bells ringing" piles up sounds so readers can hear the din.

points.label: Action verbs
points.text: "revved", "swerved", "jostled" and "dive" keep the writing fast and full of movement.

points.label: Overstatement and understatement
points.text: "eternity" exaggerates while "strong opinions" plays danger down, and both make us laugh.

overview.heading: How it is organised
overview.intro: The passage moves from a slow wait to a fast chase, then ends on a twist.

points.label: Slow build-up
points.text: "eternity" stretches the wait, so the race feels more explosive when it comes.

points.label: Chaotic middle
points.text: "two races" shows the action at its peak, with donkeys and cars racing at once.

points.label: Abrupt ending
points.text: "The race was over" is a short, blunt sentence that stops the action dead.

points.label: Final twist
points.text: "don't even have my licence" saves the biggest surprise for the closing lines.
